questions.stem: Why is PCR usually carried out before a forensic DNA sample is profiled?
options: PCR removes non-coding DNA so that only genes remain
PCR adds a coloured dye so the DNA can be seen on a gel
The sample often holds too little DNA to test directly
PCR cuts the DNA into fragments of standard sizes
questions.explanation: The polymerase chain reaction amplifies a minute amount of DNA into millions of copies, enough to analyse. Cutting DNA at specific sites is done by restriction enzymes, not PCR.

questions.stem: What happens when a PCR mixture is heated to about 95 °C at the start of each cycle?
options: Primers bind to both ends of the target sequence
Polymerase adds free nucleotides to the primers
Short DNA fragments are joined into one strand
The DNA strands separate as hydrogen bonds break
questions.explanation: Heating denatures the DNA: the hydrogen bonds between bases break and the two strands separate. Primers bind when the mixture is cooled, and extension follows at about 72 °C.

questions.stem: In PCR, what happens during the annealing step, when the mixture is cooled to about 55 °C?
options: Primers bind to complementary sequences on each single strand
The double helix unwinds as the hydrogen bonds between bases break
Taq polymerase is destroyed so that the reaction can be stopped
Free nucleotides pair up with each other to form new DNA strands
questions.explanation: Cooling lets the short primers form hydrogen bonds with matching sequences at each end of the target region. Strand separation happens at the higher denaturing temperature, before annealing.

questions.stem: Why is Taq polymerase, from a bacterium living in hot springs, used in PCR?
options: It cuts the target DNA at specific recognition sequences
It copies mRNA back into DNA so that genes can be amplified
It is not denatured by the high temperatures of each cycle
It binds the primers to the template at room temperature
questions.explanation: Each PCR cycle heats the mixture to about 95 °C, which would denature most enzymes. Taq polymerase is heat-stable, so it keeps working through repeated cycles without being replaced.

questions.stem: What is the role of the primers in PCR?
options: They break the hydrogen bonds between the two strands of DNA
They supply all of the free nucleotides used to build new strands
They cut the template DNA so the target region is released
They give polymerase a starting point at each end of the target
questions.explanation: Polymerase can only add nucleotides to an existing strand, so primers that bind either side of the target region mark where copying begins. Heat, not primers, separates the strands.

questions.stem: A forensic sample contains 50 copies of a target DNA sequence. Assuming the number doubles every cycle, how many copies are there after 10 cycles of PCR?
questions.explanation: Ten doublings multiply the number by 2^10 = 1024, and 50 x 1024 = 51,200. The figure 25,600 counts only nine doublings, and 1,000 or 500 treats the growth as adding rather than doubling.

questions.stem: Why does DNA move towards the positive electrode during gel electrophoresis?
options: Its deoxyribose sugars are attracted to the electrode
Its phosphate groups give it an overall negative charge
Its nitrogenous bases give it an overall positive charge
The gel carries a positive charge that repels the DNA
questions.explanation: The phosphate groups in the DNA backbone are negatively charged, so DNA fragments are drawn towards the positive electrode. The bases do not give DNA a positive charge.

questions.stem: In gel electrophoresis, which DNA fragments travel furthest from the wells?
options: Those richest in G-C pairs, because these bind the gel least
The smallest, because they pass most easily through the gel
The largest, because they carry the most negative charge
The largest, because their greater mass pushes them along
questions.explanation: The gel acts as a sieve: short fragments slip through its pores faster than long ones. Charge per unit length is about the same for all fragments, so size decides the distance travelled.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of running a DNA ladder in one lane of a gel?
options: To show whether the gel has fully set before the samples are loaded
To supply the current that moves the fragments through the gel
To cut the sample DNA into fragments of a set, standard length
To estimate fragment sizes by comparing with bands of known length
questions.explanation: A ladder is a mix of DNA fragments of known sizes, so the position of a sample band can be compared against it to estimate its length. The current comes from the power supply, not the ladder.

questions.stem: Fragments of 500, 1500 and 3000 base pairs are run on the same gel. How are they arranged after electrophoresis?
options: 500 nearest the wells, then 1500, with 3000 furthest away
All three level, since each base carries the same charge
1500 nearest the wells, then 500, with 3000 furthest away
3000 nearest the wells, then 1500, with 500 furthest away
questions.explanation: Smaller fragments move further through the gel, so the 500 bp band travels furthest and the 3000 bp band stays nearest the wells. Equal charge per base is why size alone sets the order.

questions.stem: What is the function of a restriction enzyme in gene technology?
options: Join DNA fragments by forming new bonds
Copy DNA strands using free nucleotides
Separate DNA fragments according to their size
Cut DNA at specific recognition sequences
questions.explanation: Each restriction enzyme recognises a particular short base sequence and cuts the DNA there. Joining fragments is the job of DNA ligase.

questions.stem: A linear DNA molecule 5000 base pairs long has two sites cut by a restriction enzyme, at positions 1200 and 3500. What fragments are produced?
questions.explanation: Two cuts in a linear molecule give three pieces: 0 to 1200 (1200 bp), 1200 to 3500 (2300 bp) and 3500 to 5000 (1500 bp). They add up to the original 5000 bp, which is a useful check.

questions.stem: What does DNA sequencing determine?
options: The total mass of DNA in the nucleus
The order of the bases in a DNA molecule
The number of chromosomes in each body cell
The size of each DNA fragment in a gel
questions.explanation: Sequencing reads the order of nucleotides (A, T, C and G) along a DNA strand. Sequencing a whole genome lets scientists map where genes lie.

questions.stem: What does mapping a species' genome by DNA sequencing allow scientists to do?
options: Remove every harmful mutation from the species' gene pool
Measure how quickly each of its cells makes its proteins
Locate its genes and compare them with other species' genes
Change the alleles that each individual passes to offspring
questions.explanation: A genome map shows the sequence and position of genes, which can then be compared within and between species. Sequencing reads DNA; it does not alter it.

questions.stem: Why does DNA profiling target short tandem repeats (STRs)?
options: They are coding regions, so they change the proteins a person makes
They are identical in every member of a species, so act as controls
They are found only in mitochondria, so pass from mother to child
The number of repeats at each locus varies widely between people
questions.explanation: STRs are non-coding sequences repeated many times, and the number of repeats at a locus differs greatly between individuals. Testing several loci gives a profile almost unique to one person.

questions.stem: At four STR loci, crime-scene DNA has repeat numbers (12,15), (8,8), (20,22) and (9,11). Suspect P has (12,15), (8,8), (20,22), (9,11). Suspect Q has (12,15), (8,9), (20,22), (9,11). What can be concluded?
options: P matches at every locus; Q is excluded by the second locus
Both match, because each of them shares three of the four loci
Q matches, because one difference is within normal error
Neither can be judged without comparing their coding DNA
questions.explanation: A profile match requires the same alleles at every locus tested, so a single mismatch excludes Q as the source. P matches at all four loci, which supports but does not on its own prove that P was the source.

questions.stem: At one STR locus a child has alleles of 10 and 14 repeats, and the mother has 10 and 12. Which man could be the child's biological father?
options: A man with 14 and 16
A man with 10 and 12
A man with 12 and 16
A man with 11 and 13
questions.explanation: The child received one allele from each parent. The 10 can come from the mother, so the 14 must have come from the father, and only the man carrying 14 could have supplied it.

questions.stem: Why can standard DNA profiling not tell identical twins apart?
options: Their short tandem repeats are lost early in development
Their DNA is identical only in their coding regions
Their profiles change too quickly to compare reliably
They develop from one zygote, so they share the same DNA
questions.explanation: Identical twins form when one zygote splits, so their genomes, including their STRs, are the same. Profiles are stable through life; the twins simply have the same DNA.

questions.stem: Which sequence of steps produces a recombinant plasmid carrying a gene of interest?
options: Cut gene and plasmid with one restriction enzyme, join with ligase, insert into bacteria
Join gene and plasmid with ligase, then cut with a restriction enzyme, insert into bacteria
Insert the gene into bacteria, cut it with ligase, join it with a restriction enzyme
Cut the plasmid with ligase, add the gene by PCR, join with a restriction enzyme
questions.explanation: The same restriction enzyme opens the plasmid and cuts out the gene, DNA ligase seals the gene into the plasmid, and the plasmid is then taken up by bacterial cells. Ligase joins DNA; it does not cut it.

questions.stem: Why are the gene and the plasmid cut with the same restriction enzyme when making recombinant DNA?
options: This removes the antibiotic-resistance gene from the plasmid
This copies the gene many times before it is inserted
This leaves matching sticky ends that can base-pair
This makes the gene and plasmid exactly the same length
questions.explanation: Cutting both with one enzyme leaves complementary single-stranded overhangs, so the gene's ends pair with the plasmid's ends before ligase seals them. The pieces do not need to be the same length.

questions.stem: What is the role of DNA ligase in making recombinant DNA?
options: It copies a DNA template by adding free nucleotides to it
It joins the sugar-phosphate backbones of DNA fragments
It cuts DNA at a specific short recognition sequence
It separates DNA fragments according to their size
questions.explanation: Ligase forms bonds in the sugar-phosphate backbone, sealing an inserted gene into a plasmid. Cutting at recognition sites is done by restriction enzymes.

questions.stem: A plasmid used to carry a gene also contains a gene for antibiotic resistance. Why?
options: So bacteria that took up the plasmid can be selected on antibiotic plates
So that the inserted gene is protected from being cut by restriction enzymes
So the transformed bacteria can be used to treat infections in patients
So the plasmid can be copied by PCR without any primers being added
questions.explanation: Only bacteria that have taken up the plasmid survive when grown with the antibiotic, so the transformed cells are easy to select. The marker gene plays no part in protecting or copying the inserted gene.

questions.stem: What is a transgenic organism?
options: An organism whose genes have been changed by radiation
An organism carrying a gene transferred from another species
An organism produced by crossing two closely related species
An organism cloned from a single cell of an adult parent
questions.explanation: A transgenic organism contains a gene from a different species, inserted using recombinant DNA technology. Crossing two species by breeding produces a hybrid, not a transgenic organism.

questions.stem: Bt cotton carries a gene from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis. Which desirable trait does this gene give the crop?
options: Tolerance of salty soils, as its cells store extra sodium ions
Faster growth, as its cells make extra plant growth hormone
Resistance to insect pests, as its cells make an insecticidal protein
Tolerance of a herbicide, so that weeds can be sprayed around the crop
questions.explanation: The Bt gene codes for a protein that is toxic to certain insect larvae that eat the plant, so less insecticide spraying is needed. Herbicide tolerance comes from different inserted genes.

questions.stem: What is the main benefit to a farmer of growing herbicide-tolerant canola?
options: Insect pests that eat the crop are killed by the herbicide gene
The crop no longer needs fertiliser, as weeds are no competition
A herbicide can be sprayed to kill weeds without harming the crop
The crop makes its own herbicide, so weeds cannot grow nearby
questions.explanation: The inserted gene lets the canola survive a herbicide that kills the surrounding weeds, which simplifies weed control. The crop does not produce herbicide itself.

questions.stem: A salmon is engineered with an extra growth hormone gene that stays switched on all year. Which category of desirable trait is this?
options: Faster growth rate
Pest resistance
Herbicide tolerance
Tolerance of drought
questions.explanation: Extra growth hormone lets the fish reach market size sooner, an example of faster growth rate. It does not protect the fish from pests or harsh conditions.

questions.stem: Rice engineered to make beta-carotene, a source of vitamin A, in its grain is an example of which type of trait?
options: Resistance to pests
Tolerance of salinity
Improved product quality
Resistance to herbicide
questions.explanation: Adding a nutrient to the edible part of the crop improves the quality of the product. The trait has nothing to do with pests, herbicides or harsh growing conditions.

questions.stem: Bt cotton growers are required to plant areas of non-Bt crops nearby as refuges. What is the purpose of these refuges?
options: They stop pollen carrying the Bt gene from reaching any weeds
They let the cotton cross with wild plants to stay diverse
Susceptible insects bred there dilute alleles for Bt resistance
They supply extra Bt toxin to kill pests that escape the crop
questions.explanation: Constant exposure to Bt toxin selects for resistant insects. Insects from refuges have no such selection, and mating with them keeps resistance alleles rare, slowing the evolution of resistant pests.

questions.stem: A herbicide-tolerance gene passes from a crop to a closely related weed species by cross-pollination. What is the main risk?
options: Insects feeding on the weed are poisoned by the gene
Weeds emerge that the herbicide can no longer control
The crop loses its tolerance and is killed by the spray
The weed becomes unable to produce any fertile seed
questions.explanation: Gene flow from crop to weed can produce herbicide-resistant 'super weeds' that are harder to control. The crop keeps its own copy of the gene.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a transgenic crop affecting non-target organisms?
options: Crop yields rise because fewer pests feed on the plants
Insects that do not eat the crop are harmed by toxin in its pollen
Pest insects evolve resistance to the toxin made in the crop
Weed species gain the crop's herbicide-tolerance gene
questions.explanation: Non-target organisms are species the trait was not meant to affect, such as harmless insects that contact the toxin. Resistance in the pest itself is a separate risk: the evolution of resistant species.

questions.stem: A single transgenic crop variety is planted across a whole farming region. Why could this reduce the crop's resilience?
options: Low genetic diversity means one new pest or disease could affect every plant
Transgenic plants cannot set seed, so the region must replant from stock
The inserted gene mutates rapidly and spreads into every other crop grown
Uniform crops always produce lower yields than a mix of older varieties
questions.explanation: When every plant is genetically the same, none may carry alleles that resist a new pathogen or pest, so losses can be widespread. Genetic diversity gives some individuals a chance to survive a new threat.

questions.stem: Water samples from a river are tested for traces of DNA from an endangered fish. What is the main advantage of this method?
options: It removes introduced fish species from the river system
It detects the species without catching or even seeing the fish
It measures the exact age of every fish living in the river
It raises the genetic diversity of the fish population
questions.explanation: Environmental DNA shed into water reveals whether a species is present, without trapping or disturbing rare animals. It monitors the population; it does not change it.

questions.stem: Researchers collect hair caught on sticky tape at bait stations and profile its DNA. What can the profiles tell them?
options: How old each animal is and how much each one weighs
Whether each animal has been vaccinated against disease
What each animal ate during the week before the visit
How many different individuals visited, without trapping any
questions.explanation: Each individual has a distinct DNA profile, so counting different profiles estimates how many animals are present. This non-invasive sampling helps monitor endangered species.

questions.stem: Before pairing animals in a captive breeding program for an endangered marsupial, managers profile the DNA of every animal. What is the main aim?
options: To pair the most closely related animals so that useful traits stay fixed
To make sure that all of the offspring are genetically identical to each other
To remove every recessive allele from the population within one generation
To pair unrelated animals and keep the gene pool as diverse as possible
questions.explanation: DNA profiles reveal how related animals are, so managers can avoid inbreeding and keep genetic diversity, which improves the population's long-term survival. Breeding close relatives reduces diversity and raises the risk of harmful recessive conditions.

questions.stem: How can DNA technology support quarantine at Australia's borders?
options: By making imported plants permanently immune to every disease
By measuring the age of seeds found in shipments of imported grain
By changing the DNA of incoming insects so that they cannot breed
By quickly identifying exotic pests or pathogens from small samples
questions.explanation: DNA tests can identify a species, even from eggs, larvae or a trace of tissue, so exotic organisms can be detected and stopped. This helps prevent the translocation of exotic species and the spread of diseases.

questions.stem: Cattle breeders use DNA profiles to confirm which bull sired each calf. Why is this useful?
options: It makes each calf a clone of its sire, so traits are passed unchanged
It stops the calves inheriting any of the alleles carried by the cow
It verifies pedigrees so breeders can select animals with desired traits
It changes each calf's genotype so that it carries the bull's best alleles
questions.explanation: Parentage testing is a DNA identification technology that confirms an animal's ancestry, which supports breeding decisions. It reads the DNA but does not alter it.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the field of bioinformatics?
options: Building and using databases to analyse biological data such as sequences
Inserting genes taken from one species into the body cells of another species
Amplifying small samples of DNA into amounts large enough to test
Separating fragments of DNA by size using an electric current
questions.explanation: Bioinformatics stores biological data, such as nucleotide and amino acid sequences, in databases and uses computers to analyse and compare it. The other descriptions are recombinant DNA technology, PCR and gel electrophoresis.

questions.stem: A gene from a newly found frog is compared with database sequences of the same gene. Identity: species W 97%, X 91%, Y 84%, Z 78%. What is the best conclusion?
options: The new frog must be a hybrid of species W and X
Species Y and Z are each other's closest relatives
The new frog is most closely related to species W
The new frog is most closely related to species Z
questions.explanation: The more similar two sequences are, the more recently the species shared a common ancestor, so 97% identity points to W. The data compare each species only with the new frog, so they cannot show how Y and Z relate to each other.
